📦 Repo: Assembly Language Dry Running Tool Project
What it is: An 8086 assembly dry-run debugger with an authentic AFD-Pro style UI — a headless virtual-CPU engine (app.js) plus a browser front-end (index.html, afd.js, styles.css, afd.css).

Structure
app.js — the core engine: segmented virtual 8086 CPU (registers, flags, memory, instruction execution)
afd.js / afd.css — the AFD-Pro debugger skin (grey grid, byte column, CP437, error line, flags colouring)
index.html — main page with AdTec splash + live DOS screen
afd-toolchain/ — bundled DOS-era tools: AFD.EXE, ALINK.EXE, nasm.exe, ndisasm.exe, RSX.EXE, plus sample .asm files and macros
tests/ — correctness suite: 10 case files (00-core → 90-rules) covering arithmetic, logic/shifts, mul/div/BCD, flow/stack, data/memory/IO, segmentation, etc.

Excellent instinct — the research paid off. Here's what I found, and you're right: it's not simple. Let me lay it out.

🔬 Research findings — the prior-art landscape
Project	What it proves	What it lacks (our opening)
x86-64-playground (732★, ISC)	Full NASM/GNU-as compiled to WASM runs client-side; GDB-like debugger (disasm + registers + memory) on a static GitHub Pages site. Tech: TypeScript + Svelte + Vite	x86-64 Linux only — no 16-bit, no DOS, no AFD, single editor page, no notebook model
v86 (23.5k★, BSD-2)	A real PC (Pentium-4-level x86) boots real MS-DOS/FreeDOS in the browser via x86→WASM JIT	Single-stepping (trap flag) is explicitly missing — fatal for a teaching stepper; huge, complex codebase; no notebook/education layer
EXACT (34★, GPL-3)	Bare-metal 8086 in raw WASM: all opcodes incl. illegal ones, segmented memory	No interrupts, no BIOS/DOS services, no hardware — bare metal only
iarm (Jupyter ARM kernel)	A real Jupyter kernel for an assembly interpreter exists	Requires a Python server — dies on static hosting; no DOSBox embedding
Your Doomsday repo	Real DOSBox (js-dos) + real NASM in browser works, with 15 documented NFRs and 7 hard-won traps	Showcase page, not a platform; no interpreter-stepping view
Conclusion: nobody has combined the three pillars — (1) notebook model, (2) fully inspectable 8086 interpreter, (3) real DOS + NASM + AFD one-click. Your project genuinely fills a gap.

⚠️ The three hard truths you sensed
1. "Fully like Jupyter" — model, not stack. Real Jupyter requires a Python kernel server (that's why iarm exists — a Python package). On static GitHub Pages that's impossible. But Jupyter's essence is client-independent: cells + kernel protocol (execute/step/interrupt) + rich outputs + save format. The correct architecture is a client-side kernel speaking a Jupyter-like message protocol, with notebooks saved in a Jupyter-compatible JSON format. Bonus: a future adapter could expose the same kernel as a real Jupyter kernel for local users — the protocol makes that path real, not hand-wavy.

2. "Engine that passes all tests to man" needs an oracle strategy, not just more unit tests. The honest ladder:

Encoder differential testing — feed every instruction form through your engine's encoder and through real NASM/ndisasm (you already ship ndisasm.exe, and NASM runs inside js-dos!). Byte-for-byte comparison = machine-checked proof your encoding is real.
Semantics differential testing — run generated test programs on your interpreter AND on DOSBox/v86, compare register/flag/memory end-states. v86 boots FreeDOS in a headless browser — usable as a CI oracle.
Then fuzzing + documented edge cases (AF/OF corner semantics, AAM with 0, boundary flag behavior).
3. The UI is a bigger deal than it looks. x86-64-playground needed Svelte+Vite for something simpler than your vision. A notebook demands: cell editing, CodeMirror 6 (assembly highlighting, gutter breakpoints, error squiggles — reusing your nasm-errors.js parser), virtualized 64KB memory hex views, timeline scrubbing, resizable panes. Vanilla JS is possible (your repos prove you like zero-build) but you'd hand-build state management that a framework gives free — and CodeMirror 6 is an npm dependency that basically forces a bundler anyway.

Phase 2 — Notebook UI: cells (asm/markdown), run/step/debug, rich outputs (register diffs, flag timeline, memory heatmap, stack view, stdout), .ipynb-compatible JSON save format, localStorage + export + share-URL
Phase 3 — DOS lane: embed Doomsday's js-dos stack (iframe-per-run pattern, NFRs, traps); one-click "Assemble & Run in real DOS" → writes source to emulated C:, runs nasm prog.asm -o prog.com then afd prog.com; live terminal pane where mount c c:\dosbox, c: etc. all work manually too; plus a fast path (WASM NASM, à la x86-64-playground) so simple assembly doesn't need a DOS boot

Great questions — let me clear both up precisely, because they're the two most important architecture facts.

Q1: Are we building a kernel for Jupyter, or a Jupyter-like thing?
Neither exactly — we're building our own complete thing. No Python, no Jupyter installation, no server.


REAL JUPYTER (what we are NOT doing):
  Browser UI ──► Python server ──► kernel (Python) ──► Python code
  ✗ needs a server, ✗ can't host on GitHub Pages, ✗ can't embed DOSBox

WHAT WE'RE BUILDING:
  Browser UI (Jupyter-LIKE: cells, run, outputs, saved notebooks)
        │
        ▼
  OUR ENGINE ("the kernel") — pure JavaScript, ported from your app.js
        │  runs 8086 assembly directly in the browser tab
        ▼
  Optional second engine: real DOSBox (js-dos) for the DOS lane
So: Jupyter is the inspiration for the interface (cells, In[1]/Out[1], markdown between code, state carries across cells) — but the whole thing is one static website. Your app.js engine becomes the kernel. It already exists and passes 375 tests; we're hardening and wiring it into this UI. The word "kernel" just means "the thing that executes cells," same role Python's kernel plays in real Jupyter.

Q2: What is the "debug view"? (the part you didn't understand)
Think of it as AFD — but built into the page and hooked directly into our own engine, so it can do things real AFD can't. When your cell runs, our engine executes your assembly instruction-by-instruction internally. The debug view is a live window into that:

Pause anywhere, or before you even start — then press Step to advance exactly one instruction. After each step you instantly see AX/BX/CX/IP/flags change on screen. This is "dry running" — your original project's whole purpose — but live and interactive instead of pre-computed.
Breakpoints — click a line number; the program runs fast and freezes when it reaches that line.
Everything visible at once: registers, flags, the 64KB memory as hex, the stack, and the DOS text screen (rendered from what the program writes to B800h / INT 21h).
Total control: while paused, click any register or memory byte and type a new value, then keep stepping — "what if AX was 5 here?" answered instantly.
The timeline: the engine records every step of the run, so you can rewind backwards through execution like scrubbing a video — see what AX was at step 30 even if you're now at step 300.
The distinction between the two debug things:

Interpreter debug view (ours)	DOSBox lane
What it is	Our own UI wired into our own engine	The real AFD program running inside real DOS
Speed	Instant, no boot	~1s boot

Three great points to nail down. Let me take them one at a time.

1. "I prefer real DOSBox to be fully authentic"
Here's the key fact: js-dos IS real DOSBox. It's not an imitation or a re-implementation — it's the actual DOSBox source code compiled to WebAssembly. When your .COM runs in the DOS lane, it runs under genuine DOSBox, in genuine DOS, with the genuine NASM 2.16.03 and genuine AFD.EXE — the same bits as your desktop DOSBox. Your Doomsday README already says it right: "It is a faster way to run the same toolchain, not a simulation of it."

So nothing is lost. The reason it's a separate lane rather than the only engine is a hard technical wall, not a preference:

Inside DOSBox, we (the web page) can only talk to it through a screen and a keyboard. We can't reach inside and read CPU registers, set breakpoints, or step one instruction — only AFD's own screen drawing is visible, as pixels.
So a notebook cell can't show a live register timeline from DOSBox — the data physically can't leave the emulated machine.
Both lanes are "real": DOSBox lane = real software, running really. Interpreter lane = real CPU semantics, re-implemented in JS and machine-verified against DOSBox (we run the same programs on both and require identical register/flag/memory results). Your instinct for authenticity becomes the testing strategy: DOSBox is the ground truth our engine must match.
2. "Is the debug view as good as the real AFD?"
To be precise: the debug view is not AFD — it's our own UI, deliberately skinned to look like AFD (grey grid, CP437, the same layout your muscle memory knows). Real AFD is included too — inside the DOS lane, exactly as you run it today (afd cpp.com).

Which is "better" depends on the job:

Capability	Real AFD (in DOSBox)	Our debug view (our engine)
Step one instruction	✅	✅
Registers/flags/memory visible	✅	✅
Rewind backwards in time	❌ impossible	✅ timeline scrubbing
Edit a register/memory mid-run and continue	partial (AFD has some of this)	✅ full, plus snapshots
Record & replay a whole run	❌	✅
Attach outputs to notebook cells	❌	✅ native
Guaranteed DOS-identical behavior	✅ it is DOS	✅ by differential testing, but it's the goal, not automatic
So the honest framing: AFD in DOSBox is the authority; our debug view is the microscope. AFD can't be beaten for authenticity. Ours can't be beaten for teaching, because rewind/edit/replay are physically impossible from outside DOSBox.

3. Extra NFRs worth defining for this project's scope
Building on your Doomsday N1–N15 style, here's the full NFR set for the notebook:

Performance & reliability

N1 — First paint never waits on the js-dos payload (~4MB): DOS lane lazy-loads only when first used
N2 — Interpreter handles 1M+ instructions/sec on a mid laptop; timeline recording is capped/ring-buffered (e.g. last 100k steps) so long programs never exhaust memory
N3 — An infinite loop never requires a page reload (Stop always works; interpreter runs in slices so the UI never freezes)
N4 — Autosave: notebook state survives crash/close/refresh (localStorage, debounced)
N5 — Boot/assemble failure always shows a real message + retry, never a dead spinner
Correctness & trust (education-specific)

N6 — Engine accuracy is enforced by CI: encoder differential vs NASM/ndisasm, semantics differential vs DOSBox — a regression fails the build
N7 — When our engine and DOS disagree, the UI says so honestly (label the interpreter lane "verified against DOSBox: X,XXX instruction forms") — never silently claims authenticity
Access & inclusion

N8 — Works fully offline after first load (PWA/service worker) — classroom with bad Wi-Fi still works
N9 — Keyboard-only operable; screen-reader output via aria-live debug log (carry over N7/N8 from Doomsday)
N10 — Works on phones (tabbed panes, never display:none on the source — your documented rule)
N11 — No accounts, no backend, nothing leaves the browser (N12 from Doomsday, unchanged)
Data & portability

N12 — Notebooks are plain JSON files, importable/exportable, future Jupyter-compatible; share links encode the notebook in the URL (works on GitHub Pages, no server)
N13 — All engine changes between runs are undoable; "reset kernel" restores a clean machine state
Legal & maintainability

N14 — License compliance: js-dos (GPL-2) + NASM (BSD-2) attribution and NOTICE file; project GPL-2 like Doomsday
N15 — Kernel stays DOM-free and node-testable; only one module knows js-dos exists (carry over N14 from Doomsday)
N16 — prefers-reduced-motion respected; graceful "browser unsupported" overlay if WebAssembly missing

How we guarantee "one pixel not changed"

Boot real AFD.EXE in DOSBox, load the same programs, screenshot the reference screens (they're deterministic for a given program+state)
Our renderer draws the same program state to a canvas

Same for font rendering: we embed the authentic CP437 VGA font bitmap so glyph shapes are identical, not "a similar monospace font"
That gives us three differential test suites, all machine-checked: encoder bytes (vs NASM), CPU semantics (vs DOSBox execution), and screen pixels (vs real AFD). "Extremely accurate engine" stops being a claim and becomes a green CI check.

which of the two optoins you gave give me pros and cons and what our project might need so i can make a informed decision

Good — this is the last big decision, so let's do it properly.

Vite + TypeScript + CodeMirror vs. Vanilla JS zero-build
First, one clarifying fact that shapes everything: the kernel is unaffected. Your app.js engine becomes a pure, DOM-free module either way — node-testable, framework-free, identical in both worlds. This decision is 100% about the UI layer.

Option A — Vite + TypeScript + CodeMirror 6
Pros

The UI you described is genuinely complex. Notebook cells (add, reorder, edit, run, collapse), outputs per cell, timeline scrubber, live-editable registers, virtualized 64KB hex viewer, resizable split panes, two lanes, modals. Hand-rolling state management for that in vanilla means writing your own mini-framework — re-render bugs (stale memory views, doubled event listeners) will eat weeks. A component model with reactive state eliminates a whole class of bugs.
TypeScript pays off exactly where this project is risky. The kernel port touches hundreds of register/memory/interrupt touchpoints. SegmentRegister, FlagWord, DecodeResult types catch whole categories of bugs at compile time — your 375 tests plus types is much stronger than tests alone. The Doomsday repo's nasm-errors.js shows you value pure testable modules; TS makes that discipline enforceable.
CodeMirror 6 is non-negotiable for the experience you want: assembly syntax highlighting, gutter breakpoints (click line 3 → breakpoint), inline error markers under the exact token (wired to your nasm-errors.js), autocomplete for mnemonics. It's what VS Code uses. Building this by hand to the same quality is a multi-month project on its own.
Prior art points this way: x86-64-playground (the closest existing project to your vision) is TS + Svelte + Vite. It's proof the stack carries this kind of app.
Ecosystem: vitest for kernel tests (nicer than your current runner, same node compatibility), easy pixel-diff libraries for the AFD fidelity tests, easy PWA/service-worker for offline NFR.
AI-assisted development (i.e., me) moves faster in it — typed, componentized codebases are much easier to modify safely in big jumps.
Cons

Build step exists: npm install, npm run build, output goes to docs/ or dist/. No more "edit file, refresh." (Vite is fast — hot reload under a second — but it's still a toolchain.)
More moving parts: dependency updates, occasional breaking changes between majors.
Learning curve if TS/Svelte-or-React isn't already familiar to you.
GitHub Pages deploys a built artifact — reviewing changes means reviewing source + built files (solvable: CI builds on push; you never commit dist/).
Option B — Vanilla JS, zero-build (your current repos' style)
Pros

Zero tooling, forever. Clone → open → works. Deploy = push. This is a real, deliberate philosophy in both your repos ("no build step, no package manager") and it has served you well.
Total transparency: every byte of the app is a file you can read. Nothing hidden behind a framework.
No dependency rot: a vanilla site built today still works in 10 years. React/Vite projects need maintenance to stay buildable.
Your existing code drops in directly: app.js, afd.js, afd.css, the AFD renderer are already vanilla — zero porting friction for Phase 1.
Smaller payload, no framework runtime.
Cons

The notebook UI is the hard part, and vanilla makes it the hardest part. Your current afd.js works because the AFD screen is one screen with fixed panels. A notebook is dynamic documents — cells born and destroyed, per-cell outputs, undo, selection, drag. Hand-managing that DOM in vanilla is where this project would realistically stall or accumulate subtle UI bugs.
Editor quality ceiling. Without CodeMirror: no gutter breakpoints, no inline error markers, no autocomplete — or you build crude versions. That guts the debug experience you explicitly asked for. (You can load prebuilt CodeMirror from a CDN without a bundler — but then you have a dependency anyway, just an unblessed one: no types, manual version pinning.)
No types = the kernel hardening ("pass all tests to man") relies purely on runtime tests.
Vanilla doesn't scale well with AI-assisted iteration — big refactors are riskier without types/components.
Honest warning: x86-64-playground chose a framework for a simpler UI than yours.
What your project specifically needs — scorecard
Your requirement	Favors A (Vite+TS)	Favors B (vanilla)
Jupyter-like notebook (cells, outputs, state)	✅✅ decisive	❌ hardest part
Pixel-perfect AFD clone	➖ neutral (canvas either way)	✅ existing afd.js ports as-is
Gutter breakpoints + inline errors in editor	✅ CodeMirror built-in	❌ hand-built or CDN hack
"Passes all tests to man" engine	✅ TS types + vitest	➖ node tests only
Rewind/timeline, live state editing	✅ reactive re-render for free	❌ manual DOM sync everywhere
Real DOSBox lane	➖ neutral (iframe either way)	➖ neutral
Offline/GH-Pages/no-backend NFR	✅ yes (static build output)	✅ yes
"Zero tooling" philosophy of your repos	❌	✅✅
Fast iteration with me as your coder	✅	➖
My recommendation
Option A (Vite + TypeScript + CodeMirror 6). The zero-build philosophy is the right call when the app's complexity fits in a few files — which was true for the AFD tool and Doomsday. This project is different in kind: it's an application, not a page. The two things that make your vision special — the notebook model and the interactive debugger — are precisely the things vanilla makes hardest and CodeMirror gives you for free. And your philosophy's real goals (no backend, nothing leaves the browser, works offline, static GitHub Pages) are fully preserved in Option A — the build step is dev-time only; what you deploy and what users load is still pure static files.

A middle path if it softens the blow: keep the kernel dependency-free plain-compliant JS (compiled from TS but usable standalone in node tests), so the engine itself retains the "pure files, node-testable" character of your current repos.

Want me to lock Option A, Option B, or adjust (e.g., Vite + TS but Svelte for components, which is closest to vanilla feel and produces the smallest bundle)?

The Hybrid: "TypeScript-first, framework-free"
The insight: "Vite vs vanilla" was really two separate choices wearing one coat:

Build tooling + language (Vite, TS) — you get types, tests, CodeMirror, bundling

What each piece is

DOM/UI wiring (cells in the document, panels, buttons, panes)	TypeScript written vanilla-style — direct document.createElement, no framework	Small typed helpers (~30 lines: el(tag, props, children)), hand-rolled but checked. The transparency of vanilla, the safety of TS.

js-dos glue (DOSBox lane)	One plain-JS module (your Doomsday dosengine.js pattern, nearly unchanged)	Preserves the rule from your own DESIGN.md: one module knows js-dos exists. It talks to the iframe; nothing else touches it.
Build	Vite — outputs static files to docs/	Dev-time only. What gets deployed is still pure static files: no backend, no trackers, GitHub Pages, offline-capable. Same deployment story as both your repos.

From Vite+TS (Option A):

TypeScript across kernel + logic + renderer (your preference, and the accuracy-critical 90%)
CodeMirror 6 with gutter breakpoints and inline nasm-errors markers
Vitest for the 375-port + differential suites; pixel-diff CI for AFD fidelity
One command deploy, hot reload during development
Nothing from the worst of either: no React/Svelte complexity, no untyped kernel, no CDN hacks.

Vanilla-TS UI means we manage re-renders (e.g., "register AX changed → update that one span"). That's fine — our UI is high-frequency-but-narrow (register spans, memory rows, canvas) which is exactly the case where targeted manual updates beat frameworks anyway. The notebook cell list is the most dynamic part, and even that is modest (a few dozen cells).

Honest answer: for this specific project — yes, with two caveats I'll give you straight, because "best" deserves scrutiny, not agreement.

Why it's the right call here
A solution is "best" relative to the goal, and your goal has an unusual shape:

The product IS inspection. The whole point is watching the kernel's internals (registers, flags, memory, timeline). A WASM or compiled kernel would be faster but opaque — you can't pause a Rust WASM module mid-instruction and expose its state to a JS UI nearly as cleanly. A transparent typed-JS kernel is not a compromise; it's the feature.
8086, not x86-64. A 16-bit 8086 interpreter in modern JS comfortably does millions of instructions/sec — the NFR (1M+/sec) is reachable without WASM. EXACT needed raw WASM because it targeted bare-metal completeness; you target teaching, where debuggability > speed.
The canvas AFD renderer doesn't care about frameworks. Pixel work is pixel work. Frameworks add nothing there; React would literally be overhead around a putImageData call.
Your team is you + me. Fewer moving parts = fewer places for the project to rot. Every dependency you don't add is a future breaking change you don't inherit.
The two places a smart engineer might deviate (straight talk)
1. The notebook cell list is the one spot where Svelte/React would genuinely help. Reactive components shine when UI pieces are created/destroyed/reordered constantly — exactly what cells do. x86-64-playground chose Svelte for less. My counter: our cell count is small (dozens, not thousands), and the heavy UI (AFD, memory, timeline) is canvas + targeted spans where manual updates win anyway. But if the notebook UX grows hairy, Svelte is the escape hatch — and the architecture keeps that door open because all logic lives in framework-free modules. Switching the UI layer later costs weeks, not a rewrite.

2. If the kernel ever needs 10× speed (e.g., running huge programs in the interpreter lane), the escape hatch is porting only the executor hot path to WASM — the kernel being a pure module makes it swappable. Not needed at 8086 scale; noted for honesty.

Against the strongest alternatives, briefly
Alternative	Why not the best here
Vite + React/Svelte UI	Helps mainly the cell list; costs transparency, adds runtime/idioms for ~5% of the UI surface. Kept as escape hatch.
Pure vanilla zero-build	Gives up types + CodeMirror for a UI more complex than anything zero-build was designed for.
v86 as the interpreter kernel	Missing single-stepping (fatal), opaque internals, can't do timeline/rewind — it's the oracle, not the product.
Rust→WASM kernel	Faster but opaque; the inspection layer is the product. Wrong trade for education.
Monaco editor	VS Code-grade but heavy and poor on mobile; CodeMirror 6 is the right size.
Why I'm confident, not just opinionated
The stack isn't really a bet on one technology — it's a layered architecture where every layer is swappable:


[notebook format]  ← stable JSON, portable forever
[kernel protocol]  ← message-based; could later become a real Jupyter kernel
[pure TS kernel]   ← node-testable, WASM-able if ever needed
[UI layer]         ← thin vanilla-TS; Svelte-able if ever needed
[canvas AFD]       ← pure pixel math, permanent
[js-dos module]    ← isolated, one file
If any single choice turns out wrong, you replace that layer — not the project. That's what makes this the best possible solution rather than just a good one: it's robust to being wrong.

Perfect timing for this — before locking, let's stress-test the scope. Here are the gaps I found when I put myself in the shoes of: a student trying to learn, a teacher trying to teach, a curious person who found the site, and future-you maintaining it.

🕳️ Gap analysis — 24 features we hadn't covered
A. Debugger depth (gaps vs. real debuggers)
Step-over vs step-into — stepping through a CALL should step over (run the whole function, land on the next line) or step into it. Real debuggers have this; AFD doesn't. Without it, tracing the Doomsday program is 723 single-clicks.
Conditional breakpoints — "break when AX == 5" or "break when the loop counter hits 100". Turns loop-debugging from torture into one click.
Watch expressions — pin "AH" or "memory at DS:DX" and it highlights the moment it changes during a run.
Logpoints — "print AX at this line without stopping" — observe a loop's progress across 500 iterations in one pass.
Profiler panel — which addresses executed most, register-usage histogram, loop detected ("this loop ran 2,304×"). Teaches performance, not just correctness — and pairs with real 8086 cycle counts per instruction (we can embed the authentic cycle tables — great teaching content: "MUL costs 118 cycles, MOV costs 2").
Run-state undo — Ctrl+Z for "I poked AX and broke everything" (kernel snapshots make this nearly free).
B. Engine realism (gaps vs. real DOS)
CGA graphics support — INT 10h graphics modes (320×200) rendered to canvas. This is huge: students write actual games with pixels, not just text. PC games of the era did exactly this.
PC speaker — the authentic beep via Web Audio. Tiny effort, massive delight; era-true games used it.
Timer + interrupts — PIT timer tick (INT 08h), so students learn interrupt-driven code, not just sequential programs.
Virtual filesystem shared between lanes — the file you save in a notebook cell appears on C: in the DOSBox lane. INT 21h file I/O (3Dh/3Fh/40h) works against it. Bridges the two engines instead of them being separate worlds.
8087 FPU (stretch) — even partial (FADD/FMUL) teaches floating point history. Defer if costly.
C. The learning layer (the biggest gap — we built a debugger, not a teacher)
"Predict-then-run" quiz mode — before stepping, the student predicts the next register state; the engine scores it. This is the proven way to learn assembly (dry-running is literally exam practice in assembly courses — your original project's soul, gamified).
Checkable cells — a cell can carry ; @expect AX=0005 CF=0 assertions that run automatically — like unit tests in a notebook. Enables self-checking exercises.
Hover-explanations — hover DIV BL → "divides AX by BL → quotient AL, remainder AH; #DIV/0 interrupt if BL=0" — an embedded, searchable interactive ISA reference where every instruction doc has a one-click "try it" cell.
Data-flow annotations — after a run, the cell shows "AX ← 5+BX, ZF set by CMP at line 3" — provenance of every value.
Visualization of memory as meaning — not just hex: view a region as string/array/stack-frames; see the string your program built materialize character by character during the timeline.
Assignment/teacher mode — notebooks with locked "task" cells + hidden tests + a "submit" that exports results. Makes the site usable by actual classrooms, which is the stated goal.
D. Reach (gaps in dissemination)
Embeddable widget — export any notebook (or single cell) as a standalone HTML snippet other sites/blogs/docs can embed, like x86-64-playground does. Every embed advertises the project. Cheap to build once the kernel is dependency-free — the architecture already pays off here.
Share-URL notebooks — notebook fully encoded in the link; a teacher sends homework as a URL. Zero backend, works forever on GitHub Pages.
Run recording → GIF/WebM export — "export this debug session as an animation" for lecture slides.
E. The quality machine (gaps in trust)
Performance regression CI — kernel speed is benchmarked per commit; a 30% slowdown fails CI (protects the 1M instr/sec NFR from death-by-a-thousand-cuts).
Golden-run corpus — every bug ever found becomes a permanent test case with the DOSBox-verified expected state. The test suite only grows, never forgets.
Public "accuracy ledger" page — a live page listing exactly which of the ~300 visible instruction forms × addressing modes are verified against DOSBox, with counts. Honest, checkable authenticity — no other emulator site does this.
Crash-telemetry-free error reports — when a run fails weirdly, "copy debug bundle" button gives a reproducible notebook state (no auto-telemetry — respects the nothing-leaves-the-browser NFR; the user chooses to share).
Where they slot into the plan
Phase 1 (kernel) stays, + items 5 (cycle tables), 6, 10 (VFS), 22
Phase 2 (notebook UI) + 2, 3, 4, 13, 15, 16, 19, 24
Phase 3 (DOSBox lane) + 7, 8, 9 (graphics/speaker/timer — in our engine, mirrored against DOSBox for verification)
Phase 4 (Doomsday + curriculum) + 1, 12, 14, 17 — the learning layer ships with the flagship content
Phase 5 (new): reach & trust — 18, 20, 21, 23
Everything else stays as locked (hybrid stack, dual lanes, pixel-perfect AFD, differential testing). This expands the project meaningfully — but note the sequencing keeps each phase independently shippable, and items 11/20/9 are explicitly stretch flags we cut first if they drag.

#	Feature	Verdict

27	Shift/rotate animations — bits visibly moving with the student's real data	✅ ADOPT — shl/shr/rol/ror confusion is universal

29	Friendly error correction — no cryptic messages: "line 12: DIV BL — BL was 0 → divide overflow (INT 0). A divisor must be non-zero"	✅ ADOPT — both assembler errors and runtime faults explained in plain language
30	Infinite-loop detection with choice prompt — proactively: "possible infinite loop: same state seen 1,000×. Keep waiting / stop?"	✅ ADOPT — smart upgrade over our plain Stop button; the prompt respects that waiting-on-input looks identical
31	Symbols window — all labels with live values during execution	✅ ADOPT (cheap, useful)

✅ Where all three AGREE with us (keep)
The core is worth building: transparent 8086 kernel + notebook + real-DOS verification is genuinely differentiated
Pure DOM-free typed kernel — called "one of the best decisions in the plan"

⚠️ Unanimous corrections (3/3 agree — we change the plan)
1. Scope → MVP gate. All three: 20 phases = 18–30 months, stall at P9–P12. Adopt the revised ~8-milestone roadmap with MVP = notebook + kernel + step/breakpoints + rewind + @expect cells + share/export + one-click DOS verify + Doomsday notebook, then a real-instructor validation gate (~week 8–12: 1–2 instructors, 10–20 students) before anything from P13+ gets built. The 20-phase list survives as the long-term map, gated behind adoption.

2. Pixel-diff CI → replaced. Unanimous false-failure trap (font rasterization across OS runners, VGA 9×16 cell duplication, DPR, blink phase). New design: primary golden = the 80×25 semantic screen (char byte + attribute byte) compared exactly; deterministic RGBA blitter as secondary; pixelmatch only for human-readable diff images. Same guarantee (pixel fidelity), stable tests.

3. Yjs pair-debugging ≠ serverless. WebRTC needs signaling; campus NAT breaks P2P. → Cut from roadmap; possible later with a tiny signaling service or manual pairing.

4. Kernel in a Web Worker from day one with execution budgets (5k-cycle yields) — jmp $ must never freeze the UI. Plus dual execution paths: fast path (no tracing) and trace path (timeline).

5. Differential testing via guest instrumentation, not screenshots: test programs write a RESULT.BIN (registers + flags + memory hash) before exiting; CI reads the file. No keyboard scripting, no OCR, no matched-breakpoint cross-engine parity (v86 can't single-step). And a four-tier CI: per-commit (fast Node tests) / per-PR (NASM encoder diff) / nightly (DOS oracle) / release (full Playwright smoke). Plus an undefined-flags policy (MUST_MATCH / IMPLEMENTATION_DEFINED / UNDEFINED) — never "fix" the emulator to match oracle quirks Intel doesn't define.

6. Notebook cell semantics must be designed BEFORE the UI — the plan's biggest unanswered question: what does a label in Cell 1 mean to Cell 2? Stale outputs after edits? Whole-program vs per-cell NASM verification? → New doc: NOTEBOOK-SEMANTICS.md in Phase 0.

7. Infrastructure corrections: IndexedDB/OPFS not localStorage · formatVersion in .asmnb schema · WASM NASM in an ephemeral worker (main() can't re-run) · share-URL only for small notebooks · perf CI = relative medians, not absolute gates · js-dos props.stop() now exists (iframe stays as isolation choice, not requirement) · "shared VFS" → mirrored project workspace, one-way sync first.

Of course — let's work through them. Here are the points on the table, with my honest read of each so you can push back where you disagree:

1️⃣ UI: Svelte vs vanilla-TS (the 3-vs-1 fight)
The reviewers' case: a notebook UI has ~10 panel types, dynamic cells, timeline scrubber, undo domains — hand-rolled state management becomes a homemade framework with worse diagnostics. By P7–P10 you're fighting your own code. My original case: canvas work doesn't benefit from frameworks; you like transparency; smaller dependency surface. My honest position now: they're probably right for the notebook shell specifically. The strongest compromise: Svelte 5 compiles away — the shipped JS is still plain DOM, no runtime framework, which preserves your transparency instinct at the deployment level while giving you reactivity at the development level. Canvas AFD/memory/timeline stays hand-written imperative either way. The part of me that still hesitates: Svelte 5's new reactivity (runes) is young; Preact+Signals is the conservative alternative (tiny, stable, just JS functions).

2️⃣ Scope gate (MVP before the empire)
All three reviewers say: build through ~8 milestones (kernel → notebook loop → teaching layer → accuracy infra → DOS lane → advanced debugger → hardening → course productization), then stop and put it in front of a real instructor + 10–20 students before building hardware/virtual-devices/dialects/frontier. The 20-phase plan doesn't die — it becomes the post-validation map. My take: this is right, and it protects everything you care about — pixel AFD, verification machine, and Doomsday all still ship early; only the exotic tail gets gated. The genuinely painful part: virtual devices, CGA graphics, and boot-sector lab move later. I think that's correct sequencing, but it's your call.

3️⃣ AFD.EXE legal problem (the serious one)
ChatGPT caught that AFD is AdTec GmbH copyrighted software — shipping AFD.EXE in a public GPL repo is a real DMCA risk, exactly the reasoning your own Doomsday DESIGN.md used against MASM/TASM. Options:

(a) Bring-your-own toolchain: the DOS lane works with whatever the user drops in (AFD path configurable); site ships NASM (BSD) only. Our own AFD-style clone becomes the default debugger — which fits beautifully, since that's the tool we're building anyway.
(b) Open-source DOS debugger in the lane (e.g., DEBUG-style clones, DOSBox debugger builds) — less authentic-feeling.
(c) Ship it anyway — I recommend against; it contradicts the license care your repos are known for. Note: a look-alike UI is legally different from redistributing the binary — the clone itself is fine. Font fix: swap int10h (CC-BY-SA) for a CC0 CP437 bitmap — trivial, zero visual loss.
4️⃣ Differential testing redesign
Their version is better than mine: guest programs self-report state to RESULT.BIN (no screenshot scraping), four CI tiers, undefined-flags policy, v86-for-end-states + js-dos-for-product-smoke. The one thing we lose: the romantic idea of "matched-breakpoint parity between engines" — technically unsound anyway (v86 can't single-step). The in-app parity checker survives as a UX feature (whole-program compare), just not as the CI backbone.

5️⃣ (Bonus) Market-gap honesty
XIDE already does NASM+AFD+DOSBox in a browser; vgath-8086 has step-backward. Our moat = notebook semantics + pedagogy + verification discipline. Doesn't kill the project — actually clarifies what to build first (the notebook loop and teaching layer are the differentiators, not the emulator plumbing).

Questions
Q1 — UI framework final call. You recommended Svelte; Gemini recommended Preact + Signals; the solo developer prefers vanilla-TS for transparency but will accept a compiled-away solution. Conditions: (a) the AFD screen, memory hex view, and timeline scrubber are canvas/imperative and stay hand-written regardless; (b) the notebook shell is ~10 panel types, dynamic cells, per-cell outputs, undo domains, virtualized lists; (c) the developer works with AI assistance (large generated diffs — does that change the framework calculus?); (d) long-term maintainability matters more than trendiness; (e) Svelte 5 uses new "runes" reactivity — is that mature enough for a multi-year solo project, or is Svelte 4 syntax a safer pin? Choose ONE: Svelte 5, Svelte 4, Preact+Signals, SolidJS, or vanilla with a formal store architecture (e.g., Zustand + h() hyperscript). Justify against: bundle size, ecosystem stability, TypeScript ergonomics, AI-codegen quality, hiring/community familiarity, and migration cost if wrong.

Q2 — AFD.EXE legal strategy. Given AFD (AdTec GmbH, 1990) cannot be redistributed: rank these options for the "real DOS" verification lane and recommend one: (a) bring-your-own: site ships only NASM (BSD-2) and the user's locally-provided AFD.EXE is injected into the js-dos filesystem client-side; (b) bundle an open-source DOS debugger instead (which ones actually exist with acceptable licenses? e.g., FreeDOS DEBUG (GPL?), DOSBox's own debugger console, lDebug (open source?), others — research current status); (c) our own AFD-styled web debugger clone as the only debugger, DOS lane runs programs but not AFD. Also answer precisely: is a pixel-accurate look-alike UI of a copyrighted program's TUI legally defensible in the ways that matter here (US/EU, a public open-source repo), and can screenshots of AFD be used as private CI fixtures if never distributed? Is there any evidence AdTec GmbH still exists or actively enforces?

Q3 — Notebook cell semantics. You flagged multi-cell state as the biggest unresolved design question. Give us your recommended concrete semantics document in mini-form: for each scenario state exactly what should happen:

Cell A defines x dw 5; Cell B does mov ax, [x] — where does x live, who assembles what?
Student edits Cell A after running A→B→C — what happens to B/C outputs and machine state?
jmp label_in_later_cell / forward references across cells
Run all — reassemble everything or reuse per-cell artifacts?
Does each cell re-assemble the whole program with a stable layout (contiguous translation unit + source maps), or maintain an incremental symbol table?
When does real-NASM verification run: per-cell or whole-program?
What does IP mean when execution spans cells? Recommend ONE coherent model (e.g., "whole-notebook = one NASM translation unit; cells are just editor views with source maps; execution = resume/rewind within the single assembled image" vs "true incremental cell execution with pedagogical symbol table"). Consider what real Jupyter users will expect vs what x86 reality allows.
Q4 — The DOS oracle. For the nightly semantic differential tests: compare (i) js-dos with a test-harness COM writing RESULT.BIN, vs (ii) v86 headless + FreeDOS + RESULT.BIN, vs (iii) DOSBox-X CLI (native, not WASM) in CI. Which gives the most deterministic results per CI-minute? What are realistic nightly test counts (hundreds? thousands?) given free GitHub Actions minutes? Is there a better DOS oracle we haven't considered (e.g., dosbox-staging, QEMU+FreeDOS, 86Box)?

Q5 — Instructor validation gate. Design the minimum viable validation: how do we find 1–2 assembly instructors willing to pilot (channels, outreach templates), what do we measure (task completion vs their current toolchain, SUS score, error confusion), and what result would justify killing, pivoting, or continuing? Deal on AFD — your call, your risk tolerance, and honestly the practical risk is near zero. PROPRIETARY-ASSETS.md stays as a guardrail for contributors, but we ship the DOS lane your way.

Now — the Jupyter problem. Let's actually solve it. First, let me state the real conflict precisely, because I think there's more room in it than the reviewers allowed.

Why "run this cell like Python" is hard
In Python, a cell executes in a namespace — x is just a name that survives between cells. In assembly, x is an address that gets fixed at assembly time. Edit cell 1, and every label after it shifts; cell 2's already-executed machine code now points at the wrong bytes. That's the whole problem in two sentences: Python has names, assembly has addresses.

But — and here's where I think the reviewers stopped too early — we have an asset none of them weighted properly: our kernel is an interpreter, not a real CPU. That gives us more honest design options than "give up and use Build/Run."

The design space — four models
Model A — One program, cells as views (ChatGPT's verdict). Honest, but strips the Jupyter feel. Too pessimistic on its own.

Model B — Fixed address slots. Give each cell a reserved region at a fixed address; edits never shift labels; true per-cell assembly. Costs: fragmented listings, unnatural for real programs, invents a dialect of assembly that lies about layout.

Model C — Instant reassembly + smart continuation. Reassembling a 500-line notebook takes NASM microseconds. So on every edit: rebuild silently; if the instruction at the current IP is byte-identical (checked via source map), execution state survives untouched; if not, offer "Restart with changes." Cheap, pragmatic — but state carries, not the cell-execution feel.

Model D — Persistent environment interpreter. Because we interpret, labels could live in a symbol environment (names bound to values) instead of addresses. Cell 1 x dw 5 binds x; cell 2 mov ax,[x] looks it up. True Jupyter feel. Costs: this is no longer real assembly semantics — addresses become fluid, NASM parity breaks, two engines to maintain.

My proposed solve: one honest trick + one honest mode
Trick 1 — "Run cell" redefined as "run to here." Every code cell gets a ▶ button with real debugger semantics: Restart machine → run from entry → temporary breakpoint at the end of this cell → show the state delta attributed to this cell (registers changed, output printed, flags touched). The In[3]/Out[3] feel is fully preserved — but every number on screen is genuinely what a real 8086 would do. Step-through, breakpoints, rewind all work inside that. This isn't a fake: it's exactly how hardware debuggers and IDEs treat "run to cursor." A cell that defines jmp start at the top or a proc can be entered directly too ("Debug from here").

Trick 2 — a second, explicitly-labeled mode: Playground. For the first weeks of a course — students wanting to try mov, add, int 21h fragments like a REPL — a per-notebook toggle into Playground mode: cells execute as fragments against a persistent pedagogical symbol environment (Model D), instant feedback, no build step. A visible banner says: "Playground: names, not addresses — a learning sandbox, not real program layout." Predict-then-run drills live here naturally. Switching to Program mode snaps back to the real thing — and that contrast itself teaches the difference between names and addresses, which is arguably the deepest lesson in assembly.

And C rides along invisibly: under Program mode, every edit triggers instant silent reassembly + byte-identity check, so the machine is never stale — students just see "✓ up to date" or "⟳ restart to apply."

So the full answer to "can a notebook run assembly like Python?" becomes: Program cells run as 'execute up to here on the real machine' (honest, NASM-parity), Playground cells run as true interpreter fragments (labeled, sandboxed). Nothing lies, and both Jupyter instincts — per-cell buttons and instant feedback — survive.

No problem — let's slow down and build the understanding together, step by step, with real screens.

Step 1: What makes Jupyter feel like Jupyter?
In a Python notebook, each cell is like a calculator line you run by itself, and results stick around:


Cell 1:  x = 5            ▶ run        → OK
Cell 2:  y = x + 3        ▶ run        → OK   (knows x from Cell 1!)
Cell 3:  print(y)         ▶ run        → prints 8
You can run cells in any order, go back, re-run. That works because Python keeps names (x, y) alive in memory between cells. x is just a name — it has no fixed position in anything.

Step 2: Why assembly is different
Assembly has no names at run time — only addresses (positions in memory). Watch what happens:


Cell 1:
  x dw 5                 ← "x" becomes, say, memory position 0120h

Cell 2:
  mov ax, [x]            ← this assembles to a machine instruction
                            that literally says "read position 0120h"
So far so good. But now the student edits Cell 1:


Cell 1 (edited):
  x dw 5
  y dw 7                 ← adding one line!
Adding that line pushes everything down: x now lives at position 0122h, not 0120h. If Cell 2 was already assembled with "0120" baked into its machine code, Cell 2 is now silently wrong — it reads the wrong memory. Python never has this problem; assembly always does. This is the entire "Jupyter problem" in one picture.

There's a second problem: what would "▶ run Cell 2" even mean? Cell 2 is one instruction in the middle of a program — the CPU can't "run just that." It runs from a start point, forward.

Step 3: The two tools that solve it
Tool 1 — The ▶ button on a cell means "run UP TO here"
We keep one real program (all cells joined in order, assembled together — that's how assembly actually works). But when the student presses ▶ on a cell, here's what the machine does:


Student presses ▶ on Cell 2
        │
        ▼
1. Reset the machine to a clean state
2. Run the program from the top, FAST (not step by step)
3. STOP exactly when the CPU reaches the end of Cell 2
4. Show: "here's what Cell 1 + Cell 2 did to the machine"
        │
        ▼
┌─ Out[2] ────────────────────────────────┐
│  AX  0000 → 0005   ▓ changed            │
│  (x was read into AX — Cell 2's job)    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
So the student experiences "I ran Cell 2 and got a result" — just like Jupyter — but every number on screen is genuinely what a real 8086 would do. Nothing is faked. And if they then press ▶ on Cell 3, it continues from there (or resets and runs down — we can offer both).

The silent helper: whenever the student edits anything, we re-assemble instantly (it takes microseconds) and compare. Machine up to date? Show ✓. Their edit changed addresses? Show ⟳ press Restart — never silently wrong.

Tool 2 — Playground mode (for experiments, like a calculator)
Sometimes a student doesn't want a program — they just want to try instructions, like testing a calculator:

"What does mov al, 250 then add al, 10 do to the flags?"

For that, a notebook can be switched into Playground mode: cells then run immediately as fragments, one after another, and names like x stay alive between cells — the true Jupyter feel. The screen shows a small honest banner:


🛝 PLAYGROUND MODE — cells run like a calculator.
Names stick between cells, but there are no real addresses here.
Switch to Program mode to build a real program.
So a course looks like: early weeks in Playground (fast experiments, no setup), then the switch to Program mode when students build real .COM files — and that switch itself teaches the names-vs-addresses lesson.

Step 4: Check — does this answer your original vision?
Your original ask was "a Jupyter-like website for assembly, view everything at runtime." Under this design:

✅ Notebook with cells + explanations between them — yes
✅ Press ▶ on a cell, see results appear under it — yes
✅ State carries as you go down the notebook — yes
✅ Everything visible: registers, flags, memory, stack, rewinding — yes
✅ One-click real DOS verification — yes (Program mode notebooks are real programs)
⚠️ One honest difference: "run Cell 2" really means "run the program up to Cell 2" — because that's the only meaning that survives contact with real assembly
Is the picture clear now? And which part do you want to dig into — the ▶ behavior, Playground mode, or something still feels off from what you imagined?

I get you now — and here's the exciting part: your mental model is not only valid, it's literally buildable. Let me play it back to make sure I have you, then show the one hard part and its fix.

Your idea, restated in machine terms
The notebook IS the machine's RAM. The CPU sits inside it at a position (IP). Editing a line = patching those bytes in RAM. Running = the CPU chews the bytes from where it is. State — registers, flags, memory — NEVER resets. It's one continuous live machine.


THE MACHINE (one, forever — like Python's namespace)

RAM:  ┌────────────────────────────────┐
      │ Cell 1: mov ax, 5       ✓ ran  │   ← these bytes ARE in RAM
      │ Cell 2: add ax, 3       ✓ ran  │   ← CPU executed them
      │ Cell 3: mov bx, ax      ← IP is│   ← CPU cursor sits here
      │ Cell 4: hlt             │  here │
      └────────────────────────────────┘
Registers: AX=0008, BX=0000... (everything left over from Cells 1–2)
Now you edit Cell 2 to add ax, 10 and press ▶ on it again. In your model: those few bytes get patched in RAM, the CPU re-runs that line with the current live state, and AX updates. Just like re-running a Python cell: x = 5 again changes x but doesn't retroactively fix y — same rule here, and it's correct.

And "▶ Run to Cell 4" = exactly what you said: the CPU starts fresh at the top and chews every line down to Cell 4, leaving the machine in that state — the prefix-execution is the feature, not a compromise. IP is simply the cursor.

The one hard part (and its fix)
Line edits change byte-length. add ax, 3 is 3 bytes; add ax, [memory_location] might be 6. If line 2 grows by 3 bytes, every line after it sits 3 bytes deeper in RAM — addresses shift under the running machine.

Two fixes, we can even do both:

memmove + relink (my recommendation): on any edit, the interpreter re-lays the code region below the edit (a fast RAM copy), recomputes label addresses, and checks the cursor: if the CPU cursor is parked at a line that didn't move, your live state is fully intact and you keep running. If the cursor is inside the shifted zone, we show ⟳ cursor moved — press Run to re-sync (never silently wrong). For notebook-style work (you edit a cell, then run it) the state survives essentially always — because you edit before running, which is exactly the Python flow.
Slot padding (optional variant): every line gets a fixed slot, so edits are literally a 4–5 byte patch, addresses never move. Costs: visible padding in the memory view (actually a nice teaching artifact — students see raw bytes + filler).
What this gives you — exactly like Python
Python notebook	ASMBOOK live machine
namespace of variables	one CPU + 64KB RAM that never resets
run cell	CPU chews from cursor through that cell
re-run edited cell	patch bytes, re-execute with live state
old results stay until overwritten	AX stays 0008 until a cell changes it
out-of-order re-runs	move the cursor to any cell, run — state applies
REPL experiments	Playground = this exact mode
import / module → real program	Build → contiguous .COM → verify in real DOS
The Build/DOS-verify story stays fully honest: the live notebook is the interpreter experience; when the student clicks Build & verify in DOS, we compile the same source contiguously like real NASM and run it on the real machine — addresses may differ from the live session (just like a Python module differs from REPL), and that's explainable in one sentence.

So: your model wins. "Exactly like Python: one live store of the entire CPU, edit a line, run that line." I'll write NOTEBOOK_SEMANTICS.md around this — live machine as default experience, cursor-as-IP, patch-on-edit, run-to-line as prefix execution, Build as the real-program exit.

One last semantic choice for you: after a student edits an already-run cell and presses its ▶ again — do you want (a) re-run just that cell on current state (my reading of your "add a line and run that"), with an explicit "▶ run from top" button for full prefix execution, or (b) always auto run-from-top down to that cell? (a) is more Python-like; (b) is more deterministic. Which feels right?

Action	How
Write assembly	CodeMirror 6 editor with NASM syntax highlighting, line numbers

//  LiveSession — the notebook's "one live machine" (R1 + R2)

//  Implements docs/NOTEBOOK_SEMANTICS.md:

\nexport type CellKind = 'code' | 'markdown';

  kind: CellKind;

powershell -Command "@'
// ================================================================
//  LiveSession — the notebook's "one live machine" (R1 + R2)
//
//  Implements docs/NOTEBOOK_SEMANTICS.md:
//   - one machine per notebook, state persists across cell runs
//   - cells are source regions of ONE assembled program
//   - ▶ on a cell = bring the CPU to the cell start, execute through
//     the cell end, leave the machine live at the cursor
//   - edits re-assemble; the machine continues when provably safe,
//     otherwise it is visibly marked `restart-needed` (never silently
//     inconsistent)
//
//  R2 adds: @expect checkable assertions, friendly errors,
//  register/flag hover docs, lesson metadata.
//
//  DOM-free and Node-testable (tests/session.test.ts).
// ================================================================
import { CPU, Parser, Executor } from './engine.mjs';
import { parseExpects, evaluateExpects, type ExpectResult, type EvalContext } from './expect.js';
import { friendlyErrors, type FriendlyError } from './errors.js';

export type CellKind = 'code' | 'markdown';

export interface Cell {
  id: string;
  kind: CellKind;
  source: string;
}

export interface RunResult {
  reason: 'cell-end' | 'halted' | 'breakpoint' | 'cap' | 'left-cell' | 'reached' | 'end' | 'restart-needed' | 'error';
  error?: string;
  steps: number;
  output: string;
  regDiff: Record<string, [number, number]>;
  halted: boolean;
  expectResults: ExpectResult[];
  allPassed: boolean;
}

export interface CellOutput {
  text: string;
  regDiff: Record<string, [number, number]>;
  steps: number;
  reason: RunResult['reason'];
  stale: boolean;
  expectResults: ExpectResult[];
  allPassed: boolean;
}

const REG_LIST = ['AX', 'BX', 'CX', 'DX', 'SI', 'DI', 'BP', 'SP'];

export interface LiveState {
  regs: Record<string, number>;
  flags: Record<string, number>;
  cursor: { cellId: string | null; line: number | null; instrIndex: number } | null;
  halted: boolean;
  needsRestart: boolean;
  totalInstrs: number;
}

export class LiveSession {
  private cells: Cell[] = [];
  private cpu = new CPU();
  private ex = new Executor();
  private outputs = new Map<string, CellOutput>();
  private needsRestart = false;
  private built = false;
  private parsed: any = null;
  private starts: number[] = [];
  private lineOwner: string[] = [];
  private bpSource = new Set<string>();
  private breakpoints = new Set<number>();
  private expectsByCell = new Map<string, ReturnType<typeof parseExpects>>();
  private cellBase: number = 0x100;

  setCells(cells: Cell[]): { needsRestart: boolean } {
    const r = this.rebuild(cells);
    this.needsRestart = r.needsRestart;
    return r;
  }

  private rebuild(cells: Cell[]): { needsRestart: boolean } {
    this.cells = cells;
    this.outputs.clear();
    this.expectsByCell.clear();
    const codeCells = cells.filter(c => c.kind === 'code');
    const parts: string[] = [];
    this.starts = [];
    this.lineOwner = [];
    for (const c of codeCells) {
      this.starts.push(parts.length + 1);
      const lines = c.source.split('\\n');
      for (const ln of lines) { this.lineOwner.push(c.id); parts.push(ln); }
    }
    const concat = parts.join('\\n');
    this.parsed = new Parser().parse(concat);
    for (const c of codeCells) {
      this.expectsByCell.set(c.id, parseExpects(c.source));
    }
    this.built = true;
    const prevIP = this.cpu.ip;
    this.ex = new Executor();
    this.ex.load(this.parsed.instrs, { base: this.cellBase });
    this.cpu = new CPU();
    this.cpu.setMem(0, 0, 8);
    this.ex.bind(this.cpu);
    this.resyncBreakpoints();
    if (prevIP < this.parsed.instrs.length && this.parsed.instrs[prevIP]) {
      this.cpu.ip = prevIP;
      return { needsRestart: false };
    }
    return { needsRestart: true };
  }

  get cellCount(): number { return this.cells.length; }
  get instrCount(): number { return this.parsed?.instrs?.length ?? 0; }

  runCell(cellId: string): RunResult {
    return this.run(cellId, 'cell-end');
  }

  runUpTo(cellId: string): RunResult {
    this.resetMachine(false);
    return this.run(cellId, 'cell-end');
  }

  private run(targetCellId: string, mode: 'cell-end'): RunResult {
    if (!this.built) return this.emptyResult('error', 'No program built yet');
    if (this.needsRestart) return this.emptyResult('restart-needed', 'The machine needs a restart because a cell above was edited');
    const targetIdx = this.cells.findIndex(c => c.id === targetCellId && c.kind === 'code');
    if (targetIdx < 0) return this.emptyResult('error', 'No such code cell');
    const before = this.snapshotRegs();
    const outBuf: string[] = [];
    this.cpu.intOutput = (s: string) => outBuf.push(s);
    const cellEndLine = targetIdx + 1 < this.starts.length ? this.starts[targetIdx + 1] - 1 : Infinity;
    let steps = 0;
    const CAP = 200000;
    let reason: RunResult['reason'] = 'cell-end';
    while (steps < CAP) {
      const ip = this.cpu.ip;
      if (ip >= this.parsed.instrs.length) { reason = 'end'; break; }
      const ins = this.parsed.instrs[ip];
      const curLine = ins.lineNum;
      if (curLine > cellEndLine) { reason = 'left-cell'; break; }
      if (this.breakpoints.has(ip)) { reason = 'breakpoint'; break; }
      this.ex.step();
      steps++;
      if (this.cpu.halted) { reason = 'halted'; break; }
    }
    if (steps >= CAP) reason = 'cap';
    const after = this.snapshotRegs();
    const regDiff = diffRegs(before, after);
    const output = outBuf.join('');
    const expectResults = this.evalExpects(targetCellId);
    const result: RunResult = {
      reason, steps, output, regDiff, halted: !!this.cpu.halted,
      expectResults, allPassed: expectResults.every(r => r.passed)
    };
    this.outputs.set(targetCellId, {
      text: output, regDiff, steps, reason, stale: false, expectResults, allPassed: result.allPassed
    });
    return result;
  }

  private resetMachine(clearBps = true) {
    this.cpu = new CPU();
    this.cpu.setMem(0, 0, 8);
    this.ex = new Executor();
    if (this.parsed) {
      this.ex.load(this.parsed.instrs, { base: this.cellBase });
      this.ex.bind(this.cpu);
    }
    if (clearBps) { this.bpSource.clear(); this.breakpoints.clear(); }
    else this.resyncBreakpoints();
    this.needsRestart = false;
  }

  step(): RunResult {
    if (!this.built) return this.emptyResult('error', 'No program built yet');
    if (this.needsRestart) return this.emptyResult('restart-needed', 'Restart needed');
    const ip = this.cpu.ip;
    if (ip >= this.parsed.instrs.length) return this.emptyResult('end', 'At end of program');
    const before = this.snapshotRegs();
    this.cpu.intOutput = (s: string) => {};
    this.ex.step();
    const after = this.snapshotRegs();
    const regDiff = diffRegs(before, after);
    const cellId = this.lineOwner[this.parsed.instrs[ip]?.lineNum - 1] ?? null;
    const expectResults = cellId ? this.evalExpects(cellId) : [];
    return { reason: this.cpu.halted ? 'halted' : 'cell-end', steps: 1, output: '', regDiff, halted: !!this.cpu.halted, expectResults, allPassed: expectResults.every(r => r.passed) };
  }

  continueRun(): RunResult {
    if (!this.built) return this.emptyResult('error', 'No program built yet');
    if (this.needsRestart) return this.emptyResult('restart-needed', 'Restart needed');
    const before = this.snapshotRegs();
    const outBuf: string[] = [];
    this.cpu.intOutput = (s: string) => outBuf.push(s);
    let steps = 0;
    const CAP = 200000;
    let reason: RunResult['reason'] = 'end';
    while (steps < CAP) {
      const ip = this.cpu.ip;
      if (ip >= this.parsed.instrs.length) { reason = 'end'; break; }
      if (this.breakpoints.has(ip)) { reason = 'breakpoint'; break; }
      this.ex.step();
      steps++;
      if (this.cpu.halted) { reason = 'halted'; break; }
    }
    if (steps >= CAP) reason = 'cap';
    const after = this.snapshotRegs();
    const regDiff = diffRegs(before, after);
    const ip = Math.min(this.cpu.ip, this.parsed.instrs.length - 1);
    const cellId = this.parsed.instrs[ip] ? this.lineOwner[this.parsed.instrs[ip].lineNum - 1] ?? null : null;
    const expectResults = cellId ? this.evalExpects(cellId) : [];
    return { reason, steps, output: outBuf.join(''), regDiff, halted: !!this.cpu.halted, expectResults, allPassed: expectResults.every(r => r.passed) };
  }

  private emptyResult(reason: RunResult['reason'], error: string): RunResult {
    return { reason, error, steps: 0, output: '', regDiff: {}, halted: false, expectResults: [], allPassed: true };
  }

  private snapshotRegs(): Record<string, number> {
    const r: Record<string, number> = {};
    for (const k of [...REG_LIST, 'CS', 'DS', 'ES', 'SS']) r[k] = this.cpu.getReg(k);
    r['IP'] = this.cpu.ip;
    return r;
  }

  private evalCtx(): EvalContext {
    const cpu = this.cpu;
    const memRead = (addr: number, bits: number) => cpu.memRead(addr, bits);
    return {
      getReg: (n: string) => { try { return cpu.getReg(n.toUpperCase()); } catch { return null; } },
      getFlag: (n: string) => { const f = cpu.flags[n.toUpperCase()]; return typeof f === 'number' ? f & 1 : null; },
      memReadByte: (linear: number) => memRead(linear & 0xfffff, 8),
      getScreenChar: (row: number, col: number) => { const off = (row * 80 + col) * 2; return memRead(0xB8000 + off, 8); }
    };
  }

  evalExpects(cellId: string): ExpectResult[] {
    const clauses = this.expectsByCell.get(cellId) || [];
    if (clauses.length === 0) return [];
    return evaluateExpects(this.evalCtx(), clauses);
  }

  getFriendlyErrors(): FriendlyError[] {
    return friendlyErrors(this.getParseErrors());
  }

  toggleBreakpoint(cellId: string, lineInCell: number): boolean {
    const key = `${cellId}:${lineInCell}`;
    if (this.bpSource.has(key)) { this.bpSource.delete(key); this.resyncBreakpoints(); return false; }
    this.bpSource.add(key); this.resyncBreakpoints(); return true;
  }

  private resyncBreakpoints() {
    this.breakpoints.clear();
    for (const key of this.bpSource) {
      const [cid, ln] = key.split(':');
      const ci = this.cells.findIndex(c => c.id === cid);
      if (ci < 0) continue;
      const abs = this.starts[ci] + Number(ln) - 1;
      const idx = this.parsed.instrs.findIndex((ins: any) => ins.lineNum === abs);
      if (idx >= 0) this.breakpoints.add(idx);
    }
  }

  getBreakpointLines(cellId: string): Set<number> {
    const s = new Set<number>();
    for (const key of this.bpSource) { const [cid, ln] = key.split(':'); if (cid === cellId) s.add(Number(ln)); }
    return s;
  }

  getState(): LiveState {
    const ip = this.built ? this.cpu.ip : 0;
    const ins = this.built ? this.parsed.instrs[ip] : null;
    const line = ins ? ins.lineNum : null;
    const cellId = line ? this.lineOwner[line - 1] ?? null : null;
    return { regs: this.snapshotRegs(), flags: { ...this.cpu.flags }, cursor: this.built ? { cellId, line, instrIndex: ip } : null, halted: !!this.cpu.halted, needsRestart: this.needsRestart, totalInstrs: this.built ? this.parsed.instrs.length : 0 };
  }

  getOutput(cellId: string): CellOutput | undefined { return this.outputs.get(cellId); }
  getAllOutputs(): Map<string, CellOutput> { return new Map(this.outputs); }

  cellLineOffset(cellId: string): number | null {
    const ci = this.cells.findIndex(c => c.id === cellId);
    if (ci < 0) return null;
    return this.starts[ci];
  }

  getParseErrors(): { cellId: string | null; line: number | null; message: string }[] {
    return (this.parsed?.errors || []).map((e: any) => ({
      cellId: e.lineNum ? this.lineOwner[e.lineNum - 1] ?? null : null,
      line: e.lineNum ?? null,
      message: e.message
    }));
  }

  memHex(linear: number, rows = 8): { addr: number; bytes: number[] }[] {
    const out: { addr: number; bytes: number[] }[] = [];
    for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) {
      const addr = linear + r * 16;
      const bytes: number[] = [];
      for (let b = 0; b < 16; b++) bytes.push(this.cpu.memRead(addr + b, 8));
      out.push({ addr, bytes });
    }
    return out;
  }

  stackView(depth = 8): { sp: number; words: number[] } {
    const sp = this.cpu.getReg('SP');
    const linear = ((this.cpu.getReg('SS') << 4) + sp) & 0xFFFFF;
    const words: number[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < depth; i++) words.push(this.cpu.memRead(linear + i * 2, 16));
    return { sp, words };
  }

  screenText(): { ch: string; attr: number }[][] {
    const rows: { ch: string; attr: number }[][] = [];
    for (let r = 0; r < 25; r++) {
      const row: { ch: string; attr: number }[] = [];
      for (let c = 0; c < 80; c++) {
        const off = (r * 80 + c) * 2;
        const chCode = this.cpu.memRead(0xB8000 + off, 8);
        const attr = this.cpu.memRead(0xB8000 + off + 1, 8);
        row.push({ ch: String.fromCharCode(chCode), attr });
      }
      rows.push(row);
    }
    return rows;
  }
}

function diffRegs(before: Record<string, number>, after: Record<string, number>): Record<string, [number, number]> {
  const d: Record<string, [number, number]> = {};
  for (const k of Object.keys(after)) {
    if ((before[k] ?? 0) !== (after[k] ?? 0)) d[k] = [before[k] ?? 0, after[k] ?? 0];
  }
  return d;
}

>> // ================================================================
>> //  LiveSession — the notebook's "one live machine" (R1 + R2)
>> //
>> //  Implements docs/NOTEBOOK_SEMANTICS.md:
>> //   - one machine per notebook, state persists across cell runs
>> //   - cells are source regions of ONE assembled program
>> //   - ▶ on a cell = bring the CPU to the cell start, execute through
>> //     the cell end, leave the machine live at the cursor
>> //   - edits re-assemble; the machine continues when provably safe,
>> //     otherwise it is visibly marked `restart-needed` (never silently
>> //     inconsistent)
>> //
>> //  R2 adds: @expect checkable assertions, friendly errors,
>> //  register/flag hover docs, lesson metadata.
>> //
>> //  DOM-free and Node-testable (tests/session.test.ts).
>> // ================================================================
>> import { CPU, Parser, Executor } from './engine.mjs';
>> import { parseExpects, evaluateExpects, type ExpectResult, type EvalContext } from './expect.js';
>> import { friendlyErrors, type FriendlyError } from './errors.js';

>> export type CellKind = 'code' | 'markdown';
>> 
>> export interface Cell {
>>   id: string;
>>   kind: CellKind;
>>   source: string;
>> }

>> export interface RunResult {
>>   reason: 'cell-end' | 'halted' | 'breakpoint' | 'cap' | 'left-cell' | 'reached' | 'end' | 'restart-needed' | 'error';
>>   error?: string;
>>   steps: number;
>>   output: string;
>>   regDiff: Record<string, [number, number]>;
>>   halted: boolean;
>>   expectResults: ExpectResult[];
>>   allPassed: boolean;
>> }
>> 
>> export interface CellOutput {
>>   text: string;
>>   regDiff: Record<string, [number, number]>;
>>   steps: number;
>>   reason: RunResult['reason'];
>>   stale: boolean;
>>   expectResults: ExpectResult[];
>>   allPassed: boolean;
>> }

>> const REG_LIST = ['AX', 'BX', 'CX', 'DX', 'SI', 'DI', 'BP', 'SP'];
>> 
>> export interface LiveState {
>>   regs: Record<string, number>;
>>   flags: Record<string, number>;
>>   cursor: { cellId: string | null; line: number | null; instrIndex: number } | null;
>>   halted: boolean;
>>   needsRestart: boolean;
>>   totalInstrs: number;

>> export class LiveSession {
>>   private cells: Cell[] = [];
>>   private cpu = new CPU();
>>   private ex = new Executor();
>>   private outputs = new Map<string, CellOutput>();
>>   private needsRestart = false;
>>   private built = false;
>>   private parsed: any = null;
>>   private starts: number[] = [];
>>   private lineOwner: string[] = [];
>>   private bpSource = new Set<string>();
>>   private breakpoints = new Set<number>();
>>   private expectsByCell = new Map<string, ReturnType<typeof parseExpects>>();
>>   private cellBase: number = 0x100;
>> 
>>   setCells(cells: Cell[]): { needsRestart: boolean } {
>>     const r = this.rebuild(cells);
>>     this.needsRestart = r.needsRestart;
>>     return r;
>>   }
>> 
>>   private rebuild(cells: Cell[]): { needsRestart: boolean } {
>>     this.cells = cells;
>>     this.outputs.clear();
>>     this.expectsByCell.clear();
>>     const codeCells = cells.filter(c => c.kind === 'code');
>>     const parts: string[] = [];
>>     this.starts = [];
>>     this.lineOwner = [];
>>     for (const c of codeCells) {
>>       this.starts.push(parts.length + 1);
>>       const lines = c.source.split('\\n');
>>       for (const ln of lines) { this.lineOwner.push(c.id); parts.push(ln); }
>>     }
>>     const concat = parts.join('\\n');
>>     this.parsed = new Parser().parse(concat);
>>     for (const c of codeCells) {
>>       this.expectsByCell.set(c.id, parseExpects(c.source));
>>     }
>>     this.built = true;
>>     const prevIP = this.cpu.ip;
>>     this.ex = new Executor();
>>     this.ex.load(this.parsed.instrs, { base: this.cellBase });
>>     this.cpu = new CPU();
>>     this.cpu.setMem(0, 0, 8);
>>     this.ex.bind(this.cpu);
>>     this.resyncBreakpoints();
>>     if (prevIP < this.parsed.instrs.length && this.parsed.instrs[prevIP]) {
>>       this.cpu.ip = prevIP;
>>       return { needsRestart: false };
>>     }
>>     return { needsRestart: true };
>>   }
>> 
>>   get cellCount(): number { return this.cells.length; }
>>   get instrCount(): number { return this.parsed?.instrs?.length ?? 0; }
>> 
>>   runCell(cellId: string): RunResult {
>>     return this.run(cellId, 'cell-end');
>>   }
>> 
>>   runUpTo(cellId: string): RunResult {
>>     this.resetMachine(false);
>>     return this.run(cellId, 'cell-end');
>>   }
>> 
>>   private run(targetCellId: string, mode: 'cell-end'): RunResult {
>>     if (!this.built) return this.emptyResult('error', 'No program built yet');
>>     if (this.needsRestart) return this.emptyResult('restart-needed', 'The machine needs a restart because a cell above was edited');
>>     const targetIdx = this.cells.findIndex(c => c.id === targetCellId && c.kind === 'code');
>>     if (targetIdx < 0) return this.emptyResult('error', 'No such code cell');
>>     const before = this.snapshotRegs();
>>     const outBuf: string[] = [];
>>     this.cpu.intOutput = (s: string) => outBuf.push(s);
>>     const cellEndLine = targetIdx + 1 < this.starts.length ? this.starts[targetIdx + 1] - 1 : Infinity;
>>     let steps = 0;
>>     const CAP = 200000;
>>     let reason: RunResult['reason'] = 'cell-end';
>>     while (steps < CAP) {
>>       const ip = this.cpu.ip;
>>       if (ip >= this.parsed.instrs.length) { reason = 'end'; break; }
>>       const ins = this.parsed.instrs[ip];
>>       const curLine = ins.lineNum;
>>       if (curLine > cellEndLine) { reason = 'left-cell'; break; }
>>       if (this.breakpoints.has(ip)) { reason = 'breakpoint'; break; }
>>       this.ex.step();
>>       steps++;
>>       if (this.cpu.halted) { reason = 'halted'; break; }
>>     }
>>     if (steps >= CAP) reason = 'cap';
>>     const after = this.snapshotRegs();
>>     const regDiff = diffRegs(before, after);
>>     const output = outBuf.join('');
>>     const expectResults = this.evalExpects(targetCellId);
>>     const result: RunResult = {
>>       reason, steps, output, regDiff, halted: !!this.cpu.halted,
>>       expectResults, allPassed: expectResults.every(r => r.passed)
>>     };
>>     this.outputs.set(targetCellId, {
>>       text: output, regDiff, steps, reason, stale: false, expectResults, allPassed: result.allPassed
>>     });
>>     return result;
>>   }
>> 
>>   private resetMachine(clearBps = true) {
>>     this.cpu = new CPU();
>>     this.cpu.setMem(0, 0, 8);
>>     this.ex = new Executor();
>>     if (this.parsed) {
>>       this.ex.load(this.parsed.instrs, { base: this.cellBase });
>>       this.ex.bind(this.cpu);
>>     }
>>     if (clearBps) { this.bpSource.clear(); this.breakpoints.clear(); }
>>     else this.resyncBreakpoints();
>>     this.needsRestart = false;
>>   }
>> 
>>   step(): RunResult {
>>     if (!this.built) return this.emptyResult('error', 'No program built yet');
>>     if (this.needsRestart) return this.emptyResult('restart-needed', 'Restart needed');
>>     const ip = this.cpu.ip;
>>     if (ip >= this.parsed.instrs.length) return this.emptyResult('end', 'At end of program');
>>     const before = this.snapshotRegs();
>>     this.cpu.intOutput = (s: string) => {};
>>     this.ex.step();
>>     const after = this.snapshotRegs();
>>     const regDiff = diffRegs(before, after);
>>     const cellId = this.lineOwner[this.parsed.instrs[ip]?.lineNum - 1] ?? null;
>>     const expectResults = cellId ? this.evalExpects(cellId) : [];
>>     return { reason: this.cpu.halted ? 'halted' : 'cell-end', steps: 1, output: '', regDiff, halted: !!this.cpu.halted, expectResults, allPassed: expectResults.every(r => r.passed) };
>>   }
>> 
>>   continueRun(): RunResult {
>>     if (!this.built) return this.emptyResult('error', 'No program built yet');
>>     if (this.needsRestart) return this.emptyResult('restart-needed', 'Restart needed');
>>     const before = this.snapshotRegs();
>>     const outBuf: string[] = [];
>>     this.cpu.intOutput = (s: string) => outBuf.push(s);
>>     let steps = 0;
>>     const CAP = 200000;
>>     let reason: RunResult['reason'] = 'end';
>>     while (steps < CAP) {
>>       const ip = this.cpu.ip;
>>       if (ip >= this.parsed.instrs.length) { reason = 'end'; break; }
>>       if (this.breakpoints.has(ip)) { reason = 'breakpoint'; break; }
>>       this.ex.step();
>>       steps++;
>>       if (this.cpu.halted) { reason = 'halted'; break; }
>>     }
>>     if (steps >= CAP) reason = 'cap';
>>     const after = this.snapshotRegs();
>>     const regDiff = diffRegs(before, after);
>>     const ip = Math.min(this.cpu.ip, this.parsed.instrs.length - 1);
>>     const cellId = this.parsed.instrs[ip] ? this.lineOwner[this.parsed.instrs[ip].lineNum - 1] ?? null : null;
>>     const expectResults = cellId ? this.evalExpects(cellId) : [];
>>     return { reason, steps, output: outBuf.join(''), regDiff, halted: !!this.cpu.halted, expectResults, allPassed: expectResults.every(r => r.passed) };
>>   }
>> 
>>   private emptyResult(reason: RunResult['reason'], error: string): RunResult {
>>     return { reason, error, steps: 0, output: '', regDiff: {}, halted: false, expectResults: [], allPassed: true };
>>   }
>> 
>>   private snapshotRegs(): Record<string, number> {
>>     const r: Record<string, number> = {};
>>     for (const k of [...REG_LIST, 'CS', 'DS', 'ES', 'SS']) r[k] = this.cpu.getReg(k);
>>     r['IP'] = this.cpu.ip;
>>     return r;
>>   }
>> 
>>   private evalCtx(): EvalContext {
>>     const cpu = this.cpu;
>>     const memRead = (addr: number, bits: number) => cpu.memRead(addr, bits);
>>     return {
>>       getReg: (n: string) => { try { return cpu.getReg(n.toUpperCase()); } catch { return null; } },
>>       getFlag: (n: string) => { const f = cpu.flags[n.toUpperCase()]; return typeof f === 'number' ? f & 1 : null; },
>>       memReadByte: (linear: number) => memRead(linear & 0xfffff, 8),
>>       getScreenChar: (row: number, col: number) => { const off = (row * 80 + col) * 2; return memRead(0xB8000 + off, 8); }
>>     };
>>   }
>> 
>>   evalExpects(cellId: string): ExpectResult[] {
>>     const clauses = this.expectsByCell.get(cellId) || [];
>>     if (clauses.length === 0) return [];
>>     return evaluateExpects(this.evalCtx(), clauses);
>>   }
>> 
>>   getFriendlyErrors(): FriendlyError[] {
>>     return friendlyErrors(this.getParseErrors());
>>   }
>> 
>>   toggleBreakpoint(cellId: string, lineInCell: number): boolean {
>>     const key = `${cellId}:${lineInCell}`;
>>     if (this.bpSource.has(key)) { this.bpSource.delete(key); this.resyncBreakpoints(); return false; }
>>     this.bpSource.add(key); this.resyncBreakpoints(); return true;

>>   private resyncBreakpoints() {
>>     this.breakpoints.clear();
>>     for (const key of this.bpSource) {
>>       const [cid, ln] = key.split(':');
>>       const ci = this.cells.findIndex(c => c.id === cid);
>>       if (ci < 0) continue;
>>       const abs = this.starts[ci] + Number(ln) - 1;
>>       const idx = this.parsed.instrs.findIndex((ins: any) => ins.lineNum === abs);
>>       if (idx >= 0) this.breakpoints.add(idx);
>>     }
>>   }
>> 
>>   getBreakpointLines(cellId: string): Set<number> {
>>     const s = new Set<number>();
>>     for (const key of this.bpSource) { const [cid, ln] = key.split(':'); if (cid === cellId) s.add(Number(ln)); }
>>     return s;

>>   getState(): LiveState {

>>   memHex(linear: number, rows = 8): { addr: number; bytes: number[] }[] {
>>     const out: { addr: number; bytes: number[] }[] = [];
>>     for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) {

>>   stackView(depth = 8): { sp: number; words: number[] } {

>>   screenText(): { ch: string; attr: number }[][] {
